lessons.title: Your first hello
lessons.objective: Introduce yourself and greet someone naturally.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Hi! I’m Maya. What’s your name?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Hello, I’m Kourosh. Nice to meet you.

vocabulary.meaning: to see someone for the first time

grammar.title: I am / I’m
grammar.rule: Use “I am” or the natural short form “I’m” before your name, country, or role.

quiz.question: Which introduction sounds natural?
options: I’m Sara. Nice to meet you.
quiz.explanation: Use “I’m + name” for a clear, natural introduction.

lessons.speaking: Hi, I’m Kourosh. Nice to meet you.

lessons.title: How are you?
lessons.objective: Ask how someone feels and answer with more than one word.

dialogue.speaker: Noah
dialogue.text: How are you today?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I’m pretty good, thanks. How about you?

grammar.title: Be + feeling
grammar.rule: Use am, is, or are before an adjective that describes a feeling.

quiz.question: Choose the complete answer.
quiz.explanation: “Pretty good, thanks” is a natural short answer.

lessons.speaking: I’m pretty good, thanks. How about you?

lessons.title: My everyday routine
lessons.objective: Describe a simple weekday from morning to evening.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: What time do you start work?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I usually start at nine and finish at five.

grammar.title: Present simple
grammar.rule: Use the base verb for routines. Add -s with he, she, or it.

quiz.question: Which sentence is correct?
quiz.explanation: Add -s to a present-simple verb after she.

lessons.speaking: I usually wake up at seven and start work at nine.

lessons.title: Things I enjoy
lessons.objective: Talk about hobbies, likes, and dislikes.

dialogue.speaker: Noah
dialogue.text: What do you like doing after work?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I love cooking, but I don’t like running.

grammar.title: Like + -ing
grammar.rule: Use an -ing form after like, love, enjoy, or dislike.

quiz.question: Complete: “I enjoy ___ music.”
quiz.explanation: Enjoy is followed by an -ing form; listen also needs “to”.

lessons.speaking: I enjoy listening to music because it helps me relax.

lessons.title: At the café
lessons.objective: Order a drink or snack politely.

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.text: What can I get for you?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Could I have a coffee and a cheese sandwich, please?

vocabulary.meaning: a list of food and drinks
the amount you need to pay
a word that makes a request polite

grammar.title: Polite requests
grammar.rule: “Could I have…?” is a friendly, polite way to order.

quiz.question: Which order is the most polite?
options: Could I have a coffee, please?
quiz.explanation: “Could I have…please?” is polite and natural.

lessons.speaking: Could I have a coffee and a sandwich, please?

lessons.title: Shopping with confidence
lessons.objective: Ask about prices, sizes, and products.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Yes, how much is this jacket? Do you have it in medium?

vocabulary.meaning: how large or small something is

vocabulary.example: The price is on the label.

vocabulary.meaning: put on clothes to test them

grammar.title: This and these
grammar.rule: Use this for one nearby item and these for more than one.

quiz.question: You are holding two shirts. What do you ask?

lessons.speaking: How much is this jacket, and can I try it on?

lessons.title: Finding your way
lessons.objective: Ask for and understand simple directions.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Excuse me, where is the train station?

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Go straight, then turn left at the bank.

vocabulary.example: The café is on the corner.

grammar.title: Direction commands
grammar.rule: Use the base verb to give a short, clear direction.

quiz.question: Which sentence gives a clear direction?
quiz.explanation: Direction commands begin with the base verb.

lessons.speaking: Go straight and turn left at the bank.

lessons.title: A smooth travel day
lessons.objective: Handle basic airport and station conversations.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: May I see your passport and ticket?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Of course. Which platform does the train leave from?

vocabulary.meaning: the place where you board a train
vocabulary.example: The train is at platform six.

vocabulary.meaning: a wait because something is late

vocabulary.example: Where can I leave my luggage?

grammar.title: Question words
grammar.rule: Begin information questions with where, when, what, or which.

lessons.speaking: Excuse me, when does the train leave?

lessons.title: Make weekend plans
lessons.objective: Suggest activities and arrange a time with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Are you free this Saturday?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I’m going to visit a friend, but Sunday works for me.

grammar.title: Going to
grammar.rule: Use be + going to + base verb for a plan you have already decided.
grammar.formula: am / is / are + going to + verb
examples: I’m going to visit a friend.
We’re going to meet at six.

quiz.question: Which sentence describes a plan correctly?
quiz.explanation: Use be + going to + the base verb.

lessons.speaking: I’m going to visit a friend on Saturday, but Sunday works for me.

lessons.title: Invite and respond
lessons.objective: Make, accept, and politely decline invitations.

dialogue.speaker: Noah
dialogue.text: Would you like to come to a concert?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I’d love to, but I already have plans. Maybe next time?

vocabulary.example: I’d like to invite you to dinner.
Maybe we can meet next week.

grammar.title: Would you like…?
grammar.rule: Use “Would you like to…?” for a warm, polite invitation.
examples: Would you like to join us?

quiz.question: Which is a polite decline?
options: I’d love to, but I already have plans.
quiz.explanation: A positive phrase plus a brief reason sounds warm and polite.

lessons.speaking: I’d love to, but I already have plans. Maybe next time?

lessons.title: Tell a short story
lessons.objective: Describe a memorable event in a clear sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: How was your trip?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: It was amazing. We arrived late, found a tiny café, and met some wonderful people.

grammar.title: Past simple
grammar.rule: Use past forms for completed actions. Regular verbs end in -ed; common irregular verbs change form.

lessons.speaking: Last weekend, I visited a new place and met some wonderful people.

lessons.title: Share experiences
lessons.objective: Talk about life experiences without naming a specific time.

dialogue.speaker: Noah
dialogue.text: Have you ever tried surfing?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: No, I haven’t, but I’ve tried kayaking.

grammar.title: Present perfect
grammar.rule: Use have or has + past participle for experiences connected to now.

quiz.question: Which question asks about an experience?

lessons.speaking: I’ve never tried surfing, but I’ve tried kayaking.

lessons.title: Clear work conversations
lessons.objective: Ask for clarification and confirm next steps at work.

dialogue.speaker: Colleague
dialogue.text: Could you send the final version by Thursday?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Just to confirm, you need the report before noon on Thursday, right?

grammar.title: Polite work requests
grammar.rule: Use could, can, and would to make requests collaborative rather than direct.

quiz.question: Which request sounds most professional?
options: Could you send the report by Thursday?
quiz.explanation: “Could you…?” makes the request clear and courteous.

lessons.speaking: Just to confirm, you need the report before noon on Thursday, right?

lessons.title: Solve a problem politely
lessons.objective: Explain a problem, request help, and agree on a solution.

dialogue.speaker: Support
dialogue.text: How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I’m afraid my order hasn’t arrived. Could you check the delivery status?

vocabulary.example: There is an issue with my order.

grammar.title: Present perfect problems
grammar.rule: Use hasn’t or haven’t + past participle when an expected action is still incomplete.
grammar.formula: has not / have not + past participle

quiz.question: Your package is still missing. What do you say?
quiz.explanation: Use present perfect for an incomplete expected result.

lessons.speaking: I’m afraid my order hasn’t arrived. Could you check the status?

lessons.title: Give your opinion
lessons.objective: Share a view, agree, and disagree respectfully.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: What did you think of the film?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: In my opinion, it started slowly, but the ending was brilliant.

vocabulary.example: In my opinion, it works well.
It was long; however, it was interesting.

grammar.title: Contrast with but
grammar.rule: Use but or however to connect two different or opposing ideas.
examples: It was slow, but I liked it.
I agree; however, there is one problem.

quiz.question: Choose the sentence with a clear contrast.
options: It was long, but it was interesting.

lessons.speaking: In my opinion, the film was slow at first, but the ending was brilliant.

lessons.title: Plan your next chapter
lessons.objective: Describe goals and the steps you will take to reach them.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.text: What would you like to improve next?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I’d like to speak more confidently, so I’m going to practise every day.

vocabulary.example: My goal is to speak fluently.
I want to improve my listening.

grammar.title: Goals with would like
grammar.rule: Use would like to for a goal, then going to for the planned action.
grammar.formula: would like to + goal / going to + action

quiz.question: Which sentence links a goal and an action?
options: I’d like to improve, so I’m going to practise.
quiz.explanation: Use “would like to” for the goal and “going to” for the plan.

lessons.speaking: I’d like to speak more confidently, so I’m going to practise every day.
